paragraphs: This checklist is for self-reflection only. It is not a hiring standard, ability score, or assessment of job competence, nor does it constitute academic, legal, or career advice. This page covers the exact U.S. O*NET/SOC occupation 19-3093.00, Historians: researching, analyzing, recording, and interpreting the past as documented in government and institutional records, newspapers and other periodicals, photographs, interviews, films, electronic media, and unpublished manuscripts such as personal diaries and letters. Official scope: Research, analyze, record, and interpret the past as recorded in sources, such as government and institutional records, newspapers and other periodicals, photographs, interviews, films, electronic media, and unpublished manuscripts, such as personal diaries and letters. O*NET lists these core tasks (24 tasks are listed, with the first 5 displayed by default): gathering historical data from archives, court records, diaries, news files, photographs, books, pamphlets and periodicals; organizing data and analyzing and interpreting its authenticity and relative importance; writing publications and exhibition content or reviewing others' writing to ensure historical accuracy; organizing information for publication and other dissemination through storage media or the internet; and conducting historical research to support identifying, preserving, and restoring historic sites and materials. Common titles include Historian, Research Historian, Public Historian, Archivist Historian, and Historical Researcher. Coverage note: U.S. wage and employment data on O*NET's 19-3093.00 page are not identified as coming from a broader or adjacent occupation; this page accurately labels them for this occupation itself (19-3093.00). In the U.S., it is in Job Zone Five (extensive preparation needed), 8.0 and above (SVP 8.0 and above). This page does not extrapolate U.S. coverage to mainland China's job titles, qualifications, or wages.

Practice brief | A wholly fictional historical-research task package, solely for practicing the process and representing no real institution, historical source, or data. Draft a plan covering: (1) how to use a fictional research topic and source leads to structure historical research: topic and question definition; source types, origins and collections; primary and secondary literature; source criticism and authenticity checks; citation and bibliography standards; oral interviews, images and digital sources; analysis, interpretation and writing; and review and publication or exhibition. Specify missing information to obtain: source access, permissions and copyright; archival confidentiality and privacy restrictions; collaboration and review requirements; and project and publication milestones. (2) How to design completion and review points for a fictional research and source record: fields and definitions, topic and source identifiers, origins, collections and versions, excerpts, transcription and translation, citations and copyright, correspondence between conclusions and evidence, and original records and revision trails. (3) How to write a handover-ready research summary: question, materials and sources—analysis and evidence—conclusions and limitations—follow-up and collaboration. (4) How to retain and use historical sources and interview data, distinguishing public information from materials restricted by copyright, confidentiality, or privacy. (5) How to pause, review, preserve records, and report upon doubts about source authenticity, copyright, privacy, collaboration or publication risks, or matters beyond your authority. Use public materials and simulated data, never real institutional or unauthorized historical-source data.

Fit signals | U.S. O*NET 19-3093.00 has interest code IC (Investigative–Conventional): Investigative means analyzing problems through evidence and research; Conventional means organizing information and data and maintaining order under procedures and rules. Core activities include obtaining information (90), identifying objects, actions and events (88), working with computers (83), processing information (79), communicating with people outside the organization (77), and documenting and recording information (76). Responsibility check | Actual fit depends on accomplishing three things within the same study: doing the research properly—using the topic and historical sources to verify provenance, critique, analyze, interpret, write, and cite, producing verifiable research outputs and source records; controlling integrity, compliance, and boundaries—working and keeping records under citation, copyright, confidentiality, privacy, and academic standards, distinguishing public information from copyright-, confidentiality-, or privacy-restricted materials and handling them under policy, and never publishing or using materials beyond authority without authorization; and accepting defined job responsibilities—being accountable for your own source handling, analysis, conclusions, and authorship, while referring matters beyond your authority or involving confidentiality, copyright, or major conclusions to the appropriate institution or personnel under policy. Test this through a verifiable experience, such as preparing a research plan and source and citation records for a fictional topic, or reviewing a response to source-authenticity, copyright, or collaboration issues, rather than relying solely on an interest questionnaire.

Direct answer | Historians on this page is the exact O*NET occupation 19-3093.00, Historians. Work falls into several categories: (i) Historical sources and research—gathering historical data from archives, court records, diaries, news files, photographs, books, pamphlets and periodicals, and conducting oral interviews and collecting images and digital sources. (ii) Organization and criticism—organizing data, analyzing and interpreting its authenticity and relative importance, and conducting source criticism and provenance checks. (iii) Analysis, interpretation and writing—organizing and writing information for publication and dissemination through storage media or the internet, and interpreting its meaning for others. (iv) Publication, exhibitions and review—writing publication and exhibition content or reviewing others' writing to ensure historical accuracy. (v) Research support and projects—conducting historical research to support identifying, preserving, and restoring historic sites and materials, and participating in research topics, projects, collaboration, and review.
